table.text: The preregistered power analyses were based on an earlier analysis plan involving oneway Analysis of Variances (ANOVA), bivariate correlations, and multiple regression. The largest resulting target was 127 participants, providing 80% power to detect small-moderate effect sizes (f² = 0.15-40) at α = .05. After inspecting the distribution and measurement properties of the primary outcome, we replaced the planned linear analyses with binomial generalised linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), which were more appropriate for repeated dichotomous responses (0 = not endorsed,1 = endorsed). Given N = 127 and dichotomous endorsement outcomes, we conducted a sensitivity analysis for logistic regression. Across plausible baseline endorsement rates, the design had adequate power to detect small-tomoderate effects at α = .05.

table.title: Autism-related language preferences of Turkish-speaking autistic adults
table.research_questions:
H1: Participants will prefer the terms related to the medical model of disability over the social model of disability, such as "person with autism (otizmli birey)" and "autism spectrum disorder (otizm spektrum bozukluğu)" over "autistic person (otistik birey)" and "autism (otizm)", respectively.

H2: A preference toward medical-focused terms will be related to lower levels of autism-related knowledge and awareness, less pronounced autism-related social identity, and higher levels of autism-related stigma.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
This study will use a mixed-method approach, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative methods to explore language preferences regarding autism among Turkish-speaking individuals. This study will be conducted through the online Qualtrics platform, using multiple-choice questions, open-ended questions, and Likert-type scales. This study is expected to take 30 minutes to 1 hour to complete.

Ethical approval and consent: The project is approved by the Social and Life Sciences Ethical Committee of Karadeniz Technical University (KTU) in Turkiye (20.11.2024 tarihli ve E-26014373-050.01.04-586889 sayılı yazı ile / Doğrulama Kod: B1210873-8CED-4707-BC90-2AE633FD088C / Doğrulama Adres: https://www.turkiye.gov.tr/karadeniz-teknik-universitesi-ebys). All participants will be expected to read and approve the Participant Information and Consent Forms before proceeding with the questionnaire pack.

Additionally, with this project, we aim:
1) to establish an "Autism Advisory Group - Otizm-Özne Danışma Grubu" under KTU, where autistic people are actively involved in all stages of scientific research related to autism, their opinions and critiques are considered, and participatory research methods are applied.

2) to create an "Autism Research Database" under KTU, consisting of autistic adults (at least 18 years old) who voluntarily provide their demographics and contact information, which is maintained and used for scientific purposes when necessary, to facilitate the conduct of autism studies.

This project includes four main steps:

1. Translation
The "Autism Related Language Preferences Form" will first be translated into Turkish, then back into English, and any discrepancies between the translations will be resolved, and the form will be finalized in Turkish.

2. The project will be set up for data collection in the Qualtrics online platform, with the following sequence and materials:
a. Participant Information Form
b. Participant Consent Form
c. Demographics Form
d. Autism-Related Language Preferences Form
e. Autism-Related Knowledge and Awareness Questionnaire
f. Autism-Related Internalized Stigma Questionnaire
g. Autism-Related Social Identity Questionnaire
h. Adult Autism Spectrum Questionnaire (AQ–50)
i. Feedback Form

Materials
The forms and questionnaires used in this project are listed below:

c. Demographics Form
Participants will be asked about their demographic information, including age, gender, ethnic background, native language(s), other languages spoken, country of birth, country of residence, length of residence in the country of current residence, educational level, and socioeconomic status. There will also be specific questions regarding their diagnoses: whether they have received a diagnosis, the nature of the diagnosis, and their age at diagnosis. Individuals who self-identify as autistic will also be included in the study. A diagnosis option will be provided for these individuals, and data analyses will be conducted both including and excluding these participants, with results compared. If the results do not significantly differ statistically, the data will be analyzed and reported as a whole.

d. Autism-Related Language Preferences Form
The original form used by Keating et al. (2023) consists of a total of 9 questions, including both multiple-choice and open-ended questions. The 8 multiple-choice questions with an "Other" option asking autism-related language preferences are as follows:
(1) When talking about autism,
(2) When addressing someone diagnosed with autism,
(3) When talking about the identity of someone diagnosed with autism,
(4) When talking more broadly about autism,
(5) When discussing challenges related to autism,
(6) When talking about the strengths of autism,
(7) When addressing individuals who are not diagnosed with autism,
(8) Whether autism can be conceptually separated from autistic individuals (yes, no, other).
Relatively new terms related to autism, such as "profound autism," will be included in the present project. For multiple-choice questions, participants will be prompted with: "Please select the terms you are comfortable using when [discussing autism]. You can choose as many terms as you like." Additionally, there will be one open-ended question:
(9) Participants can share any further thoughts on language preferences without time or word limits.

e. Autism-Related Knowledge and Awareness Questionnaire
Originally developed by Flood et al. (2013) and adapted into Turkish as the "Social Attitudes Toward Autism Spectrum Disorders Questionnaire" (OYTTÖ) by Batum and Aydın (2021), this scale is used to measure social attitudes toward people with autism. It contains 26 items, such as "Individuals with autism should not have children." Responses are rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 – Strongly Disagree, 4 – Strongly Agree). In a study conducted in Australia (Bury et al., 2023), researchers used a similar questionnaire, the "Autism Awareness Scale (AAS)," which has not yet been adapted into Turkish. Therefore, we will use a similar questionnaire described above (OYTTÖ) which is available in Turkish at the moment.

f. Autism-Related Internalized Stigma Questionnaire
The original questionnaire, the Internalized Stigma of Mental Illness Inventory (ISMI; Ritsher et al., 2003), has been adapted into Turkish as the "Internalized Stigma of Mental Illness Scale" (RHİDÖ; Ersoy & Varan, 2007). This questionnaire has been adapted for use with various health conditions (e.g., Boyd et al., 2014). Following the method of Bury et al. (2023), the term "mental illness" will be replaced with "autism." In Turkish. This scale contains items such as "People discriminate against me because I am autistic." and is rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 – Strongly Disagree, 4 – Strongly Agree).

g. Autism Related Social Identity Questionnaire
The social identity questionnaire, originally the "In-group Identification Scale" (Leach et al., 2008), will be used for autism. The original questionnaire has been adapted for use in Turkish in various research domains (e.g., Balaban, 2013). In the original questionnaire, the target concept section is left blank. This section will be filled with autism-related items. The questionnaire will include statements such as "I feel a connection with other [autistic people]." and "I feel solidarity with [autistic people]." rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 – Strongly Disagree, 7 – Strongly Agree).

h. Adult Autism Spectrum Questionnaire (AQ–50)
This questionnaire, originally developed by Baron-Cohen et al. (2001) as the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ), was adapted into Turkish by Kose et al. (2010). It covers areas such as social skills, attention shift, attention to detail, communication, and imagination, as outlined in the diagnostic criteria for autism. The self-report questionnaire consists of 50 items and is rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 – Strongly Agree, 4 – Strongly Disagree).

table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants from all genders, ethnic backgrounds, countries, and socioeconomic levels (e.g., education, income) will be included in the study. This diversity will ensure as varied a sample as possible. Participants will be individuals who are at least 15 years old, are either diagnosed with autism, are in the process of receiving a diagnosis, or self-identify as autistic. Participants will not be excluded based on co-existing conditions and/or any kind of drug use.

To participate, participants must:
• Be fluent in Turkish.
• Have received a formal autism diagnosis, be in the process of a formal diagnosis, or self-identify as autistic.
• Be at least 15 years old.

Research Link and/or QR Code: To find participants, the research link and QR code will be distributed through various channels, including:
• Institutions and organizations, such as universities
• Online platforms (e.g., Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn)
• Autism associations and organizations (e.g., Tohum Autism Foundation, Otizm Meclisi)
• KTU Medical Faculty participant pool
table.sample_size: A total of 140 participants will be targeted to account for a 10% participant dropout rate.
table.sample_size_rationale:
A mixed-methods approach will be adopted, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods (Tashakkori & Creswell, 2007). The sample sizes of similar projects conducted in other languages vary widely: 654 participants in a global study in English (Keating et al., 2023), 541 participants in France (Geelhand et al., 2023), 1026 participants in the Netherlands (Buijsman et al., 2023), 215 participants in Belgium (Bosman & Thijs, 2024), and 198 participants in Australian projects (Bury et al., 2020, 2023). To ensure statistical power for the analyses in this study, the necessary sample size was calculated using G*Power 3.1 software. Power analysis was conducted separately for ANOVA, bivariate correlation, and multiple regression analyses. The required sample sizes to achieve 80% statistical power (α = 0.05) for each analysis are as follows:

• One-way ANOVA: Used to test differences between language preference groups. Based on previous studies (Keating et al., 2023), power analysis was performed with an effect size of Cohen’s f² = 0.40. The minimum required sample size for this analysis is 66 participants.
• Bivariate correlation analysis: Used to test the linear relationships between language preferences and other variables, such as levels of autism-related knowledge, social identity, and internalized stigma. Power analysis was performed with an effect size of Cohen’s r = 0.25. The minimum required sample size is 123 participants.
• Multiple regression analysis: Used to analyze predictor variables. Based on similar previous studies (Bury et al., 2023), an effect size of Cohen’s f² = 0.15 was assumed. The required minimum sample size is 127 participants.

table.statistical_tests:
1. Quantitative analysis
Language preferences: Cochran's Q test will be used for quantitative data from the language preference form. This test is specifically designed for within-subjects binary data (where participants indicate whether they are willing to use each term or not). If Cochran's Q test shows significant differences, we will then conduct follow-up McNemar's tests with appropriate multiple comparison adjustments to determine which specific terms were significantly more/less popular than others. The analysis will be performed separately for the entire sample and subgroups (formally diagnosed and self-diagnosed). If no significant differences are found between the groups, the results will be reported for the entire sample.
In-depth understanding of language preferences: Bivariate correlation analysis will first be used to examine the relationships between demographic information, autism knowledge, and awareness, internalized stigma, social identity related to autism, and language preferences. Following this, multiple regression analysis will be used to analyze predictor variables. Interaction effects between variables will be assessed using the PROCESS macro extension in SPSS.

2. Qualitative analysis
Responses to the open-ended question in the Autism Related Language Preferences Form and responses to "Other" options will be manually coded using appropriate qualitative software. A Reflective Inductive Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) will be used to examine these responses and identify the underlying reasons for language preferences.

3. Mixed-method analysis
The parallel approach (Teddlie & Tashakkori, 2009) will be used to analyze the quantitative and qualitative data separately, followed by comparing the statistical findings from the quantitative analysis with the thematic findings from the qualitative analysis. The overall trends and underlying reasons for language preferences will be explored.

c. Demographics Form
Participants will be asked about their demographic information, including age, gender, ethnic background, native language(s), other languages spoken, country of birth, country of residence, length of residence in the country of current residence, educational level, and socioeconomic status. There will also be specific questions regarding their diagnoses: whether they have received a diagnosis, the nature of the diagnosis, and their age at diagnosis. Individuals who self-identify as autistic will also be included in the study. A diagnosis option will be provided for these individuals, and data analyses will be conducted both including and excluding these participants, with results compared. If the results do not significantly differ statistically, the data will be analyzed and reported as a whole.

d. Autism-Related Language Preferences Form
The original form used by Keating et al. (2023) consists of a total of 9 questions, including both multiple-choice and open-ended questions. The 8 multiple-choice questions with an \"Other\" option asking autism-related language preferences are as follows:
(1) When talking about autism,
(2) When addressing someone diagnosed with autism,
(3) When talking about the identity of someone diagnosed with autism,
(4) When talking more broadly about autism,
(5) When discussing challenges related to autism,
(6) When talking about the strengths of autism,
(7) When addressing individuals who are not diagnosed with autism,
(8) Whether autism can be conceptually separated from autistic individuals (yes, no, other).
Relatively new terms related to autism, such as \"profound autism,\" will be included in the present project. For multiple-choice questions, participants will be prompted with: \"Please select the terms you are comfortable using when [discussing autism]. Originally developed by Flood et al. (2013) and adapted into Turkish as the \"Social Attitudes Toward Autism Spectrum Disorders Questionnaire\" (OYTTÖ) by Batum and Aydın (2021), this scale is used to measure social attitudes toward people with autism. It contains 26 items, such as \"Individuals with autism should not have children.\" Responses are rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 – Strongly Disagree, 4 – Strongly Agree). In a study conducted in Australia (Bury et al., 2023), researchers used a similar questionnaire, the \"Autism Awareness Scale (AAS),\" which has not yet been adapted into Turkish. The social identity questionnaire, originally the \"In-group Identification Scale\" (Leach et al., 2008), will be used for autism. text.text: Autism-related terminology is contested, and preferences vary across linguistic and cultural contexts.
However, evidence from Turkish-speaking autistic communities is currently limited.
This mixed-methods study examined terminology preferences among 127 native Turkishspeaking autistic participants aged 15-66 years.
Participants selected all terms they felt comfortable using across seven categories of autism-related language.
Eighty-one participants also provided open-ended responses, which were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis.
Participants most frequently endorsed otizm ("autism"; 79.30%) as the nomenclature of autism and nörolojik/beyin farklılığı ("neurological/brain difference"; 77.49%) as a broader conceptualisation.
Farklılıklar ("differences") was the most frequently endorsed term for both autism-related difficulties (82.45%) and strengths (71.19%).

No single expression for an autistic person was endorsed by majority: otistik ("autistic"; 49.33%), nöroçeşitli kişi ("neurodivergent person"; 47.40%), and otizmli ("[person] with autism"; 45.48%) received similar support.
Individual-difference measures showed few consistent associations with terminology endorsement after correction for multiple comparisons.
Six qualitative themes concerned autonomy, social impact, identity, accuracy, context, and respect.
Turkish-speaking autistic adults generally favoured direct and non-deficit-oriented language while emphasising individual choice.
Researchers and professionals should therefore ask about personal preferences whenever possible and avoid imposing a single terminology on the wider community.
Recent years have seen scholarly, and at times political, debate around the terminology used when talking about autism 1 and autistic people 2 .
Central to this debate is the distinction between identity-first language (IFL; e.g., "autistic person") and person-first language (PFL; e.g., "person with autism").

In a large multinational survey of English-speaking autistic adults, primarily from Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, the United Kingdom (UK), and the United States (US), "autistic person" (79.5%) and "is autistic" (85.0%) were endorsed by more participants than "person with autism" (23.9%) and "has autism" (39.1%; Keating et al., 2023).

text.text: The present mixed-methods study investigated autism-related language preferences among Turkish-speaking autistic adults and examined the considerations underlying those preferences.

We asked Turkish-speaking autistic adults the terms they feel comfortable using when talking about: (1) nomenclature of autism; (2) an autistic person; (3) someone's autistic identity; (4) autism more broadly; (5) challenges of autistic people; (6) strengths of autistic people; and (7) people without a diagnosis of autism.

We also examined whether endorsement was associated with participants' self-reported levels of (1) autistic traits; (2) negative attitudes towards autism; (3) internalised autism stigma; and (4) autism in-group identification.

Given the prominence of deficit-oriented terminology in Turkish clinical and educational settings, we anticipated relatively greater endorsement of deficit-oriented expressions than differenceoriented expressions.

We further expected that endorsement of deficit-oriented terminology to be negatively associated with self-reported levels of autistic traits and autism in-group identification and positively associated with negative attitudes towards autism and internalised autism stigma.
Open-ended responses were analysed to identify how participants further explained and conceptualised their preferences.

This study was pre-registered prior to data collection (https://osf.io/x2vf3) and approved by the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Ethical Review Committee at [blinded] (Verification Code: [blinded]).

text.text: The preregistered power analyses were based on an earlier analysis plan involving oneway Analysis of Variances (ANOVA), bivariate correlations, and multiple regression.
The largest resulting target was 127 participants, providing 80% power to detect small-moderate effect sizes (f² = 0.15-40) at α = .05.

After inspecting the distribution and measurement properties of the primary outcome, we replaced the planned linear analyses with binomial generalised linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), which were more appropriate for repeated dichotomous responses (0 = not endorsed,1 = endorsed).
Given N = 127 and dichotomous endorsement outcomes, we conducted a sensitivity analysis for logistic regression.
Across plausible baseline endorsement rates, the design had adequate power to detect small-tomoderate effects at α = .05.
The sample comprised 127 native Turkish-speakers aged 15-66 years (M = 25.17, SD = 8.79), recruited through in-person (N = 54) or online (N = 73).

text.text: Seven multiple-response categories assessed preferences for autism-related terminology across different communicative contexts: (1) the nomenclature of autism, (2) referring to someone with an autism diagnosis, (3) talking about someone's autistic identity, (4) talking about autism more broadly, (5) talking about challenges related to autism, (6) talking about strengths related to autism, and (7) referring to someone without an autism diagnosis.
Each category included an "Other" option presented with a free-text field.

Where helpful, response options were accompanied by an example sentence from everyday use.
For instance, for the term "autistic person," the option was accompanied by a sentence of "I met an autistic person today."

text.text: Participants completed the study in two parts: The first part consisted of the information sheet, consent form, language preference survey and a demographics questionnaire asking participants' age, gender, native language, and related background information.

The second part included a set of questionnaires administered in a randomized order; assessing autistic traits, negative attitudes towards autism, internalized autism-related stigma, and autism ingroup identification.
Participants were recruited both online, including X and Reddit, and through clinical services across multiple regions in Türkiye, including Istanbul, Ankara, Konya, and Trabzon.
Online participants completed the study through Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/), while participants recruited in clinical settings completed a penand-paper version in-person.

text.text: All analyses were conducted in R. Quantitative analyses examined endorsement of autism-related terminology using GLMMs with a binomial link function, given the dichotomous nature of endorsement responses (0 = not endorsed,1 = endorsed), using the glmmTMB package.

To assess whether the probability of endorsement differed across autismrelated terms, a series of GLMMs, one for each category of terminology, was fitted with endorsement as the dependent variable, terminology entered as a categorical fixed effect, and participant ID as a random intercept [glmmTMB(Endorsement ~ terminology + (1 | ID))].
To examine individual-difference associations, while retaining the maximum available data, two additional sets of category-specific GLMMs were fitted.

First, a combined model included negative attitudes towards autism, internalised stigma, and autism in-group identification, together with the interaction between terminology and each predictor Models were estimated using maximum likelihood estimation, and continuous predictors were z-standardised across all available respondents before model-specific complete-case samples were selected.
Sum-to-zero contrasts were used for terminology so that predictor main effects represented associations averaged equally across terms.
Overall effects of terminology and terminology × predictor interactions were evaluated using Type III Wald chi-square tests via car package.
Average predictor trends and term-specific slopes were estimated using emmeans package.

Pairwise comparisons between terms were conducted with Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) false discovery rate correction, since this adjustment maintains greater power while controlling Type I Error, and is recommended for scenarios where there are numerous tests (e.g., 16-64 pairwise comparisons) (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995; Chen et al., 2017; Glickman et al., 2014; Hollestein et al., 2021; Lydersen, 2024; McDonald, 2014).

Themes were not mutually exclusive, and many responses contributed to multiple themes.
Collectively, they illustrate that autism-related terminology extends beyond word choice to reflect broader autonomy, identity, stigma, accuracy, and social context.
Autonomy emerged as the most prevalent theme, appearing in 78% of responses.
Participants consistently emphasised that autistic people should have the right to decide how they describe themselves, rejecting the idea that there is a single correct way to talk about autism.
Terminology was framed as a personal choice shaped by lived experience rather than something to be prescribed by clinicians, researchers, advocacy organisations, or wider society.

Many participants expressed frustration at having their preferred terminology questioned or corrected by others: "Whatever I say, I'm the one living this -being corrected by someone else saying 'that's not the right word' makes me angry."

Others extended this critique beyond interpersonal interactions, arguing that autism terminology is often shaped by institutional and professional interests rather than autistic voices: "Most of the concepts preferred and imposed by medical, academic, and civil society actors serve to reinforce discourses determined by people who profit from how autism is discussed."
Although participants often held strong personal preferences, many simultaneously emphasised that no single terminology should be imposed on everyone.
Instead, they framed self-identification as an individual right, recognising that different autistic people may legitimately choose different ways of describing themselves.

"I dislike person-with-autism type expressions that, as recommended by ridiculous organisations abroad, portray autism as something separate from the individual -a disease to be eliminated rather than a part of who they are.
But it is everyone's own choice."
(P19) Subtheme: Rejection of externally imposed terminology

Participants frequently rejected terminology that they perceived as imposed through medical, historical, or normative frameworks rather than emerging from autistic people's own understanding of themselves.
Person-first language, deficit-oriented terminology, and historically contested labels were all criticised because they were seen as reflecting external assumptions about autism.

The rejection of person-first language often centred on the idea that it separates autism from the individual and frames it as an illness or problem to be removed: "Saying 'person with autism' sounds like saying 'leper' -as though it were an acquired illness.
But it is simply a difference."

(P53) Several participants also rejected the continued use of the Asperger label, linking it to its historical origins and the hierarchical distinctions embedded within it: "I dislike Asperger syndrome and the terms derived from it, because they were invented by the Nazi doctor Hans Asperger to separate individuals on the autism spectrum into those who would and would not be useful to the Nazi regime.
For this reason, I believe these terms imply -even if unintentionally -being 'superior' to other individuals on the autism spectrum."
(P9) "I strongly reject being referred to by this name -I wish my doctor had known this too.
The screening work … aimed to separate autistic people into those deemed 'useful' -it is horrifying."
Theme 2: Words Matter Because of How People Use Them (Social Impact).
The social impact of autism-related terminology emerged in 70% of responses.
Participants consistently described the language as acquiring meaning through how it is used within society rather than through the words themselves.
Many explained that terms such as autistic had become associated with bullying, mockery, and ableist attitudes, shaping how they felt about using these labels to describe themselves.
Beyond describing the effects of stigma, some participants argued that the problem lay in ableist attitudes rather than in the terminology itself.

They suggested that replacing one label with another would do little to improve autistic people's experiences unless broader social perceptions also changed: "The reason the word autistic is seen as problematic is because autistic people are subjected to stigma.
We do not need to change the word autistic -we need to change the stigma and ableist ideology."

Others actively reclaimed the word autistic as a way of challenging prejudice rather than avoiding it: Identity emerged as a central influence on participants' terminology preferences, appearing in 70% of responses.
Many described autism as an integral part of who they are, rejecting language that positioned it as something separate from themselves.
For these participants, terminology was not simply descriptive but reflected how they understood their own identity.
"I accept the word autistic as part of my existence."

(P71) "Because I see autism as an important part of a person's identity, I do not find expressions such as 'person with autism' or 'has autism' appropriate, as these expressions portray autism as a condition that exists separately from identity."
(P34) At the same time, participants emphasised that autism represented only one aspect of a broader, multidimensional identity.
While recognising its importance, they resisted being reduced to a diagnostic label.
"No matter how much ASD affects my life, I do not think a psychiatric diagnosis captures all of my characteristics.
It is one aspect of me, but an important one that influences all other aspects of my life."
A smaller number of participants distanced themselves from autism as an identity category altogether, preferring to describe themselves more broadly in terms of difference:
Accuracy emerged as an important consideration in participants' terminology preferences, appearing in 42% of responses.
Participants consistently favoured language that they felt reflected autistic experience honestly, rejecting terminology they perceived as euphemistic, minimising, or overly simplistic.
Many participants critiqued language that appeared to soften autism in an attempt to sound more respectful.
Rather than reducing stigma, they argued that these expressions implied that autism was something negative that required linguistic cushioning.

"Expressions like 'child with autism' and 'special child' are among my least favourite, because they feel like words produced by neurotypicals who think the situation is negative and pitiful and are trying to soften it."
(P65) "When non-autistic people talk about autistic people, they tend to censor, sanitise, and overcompensate -as though there is something shameful that needs to be hidden."
Subtheme 2: Critique of functioning labels and rigid classification
Participants also questioned terminology that categorised autistic people according to perceived levels of functioning.
These labels were viewed as overly simplistic, and, in some cases, harmful because they obscured individual differences and support needs.
"I don't like being called 'mild' or 'severe' because these labels constantly minimised the difficulties I experience, my barriers are overlooked, and I cannot get support."
(P16) "I am against labels such as Asperger and high-functioning because they create an artificial divide among autistic people based on criteria determined by neurotypicals."

(P4) Subtheme 3: Preference for specificity and needs-based terminology Rather than broad or hierarchical labels, many participants preferred terminology that more accurately reflected individual circumstances and support requirements.
"Rather than high/low functioning, I prefer high/low support needs."
(P33) "I am uncomfortable with autism being seen as a disability...
I would prefer autistic people to be seen as individuals who need support."

text.text: Rather than expressing a single preferred label, many described adapting their language according to their audience, communicative goals, language, or anticipated social reactions.

Some participants used the terms they personally considered imperfect because they were more familiar or attracted less stigma in particular situations: "Asperger feels like a safer way to express it."
(P49) "High functioning isn't ethically ideal, but it's necessary to use so people understand I don't need support."
Others prioritised communication over ideological consistency, choosing whichever terminology they believed would be most easily understood:
Language itself also shaped terminology preferences.
Several participants described using different terms across Turkish and English because some concepts felt more natural or established in one language than the other.
Theme 6: Just Respect How People Want to Describe Themselves (Respect).
Respect for individual terminology preferences emerged as a distinct, although less prevalent, theme (15%).
While participants often expressed strong personal opinions about autism-related language, many also emphasised that these preferences should not be imposed on others.
Instead, they argued that autistic people should be free to choose the terminology that feels most appropriate to them:
This study investigated autism-related terminology preferences among Turkishspeaking autistic adults and examined the individual, social, and contextual considerations underlying these preferences.
Overall, participants showed a strong preference for terminology that conceptualised autism as a neurological difference rather than a disease or deficit.
However, no single way of referring to an autistic person was endorsed by a clear majority.
The qualitative findings helped contextualise the variability in participants' responses.
Participants viewed terminology as an issue of autonomy, identity, social impact, accuracy, context, and respect.
The individual-difference hypotheses received mixed support.

Negative attitudes towards autism, internalised stigma, and autism in-group identification showed several selective associations with endorsement, whereas autistic traits were not significantly associated with terminology preferences in the smaller AQ sub-sample.
The findings highlight both a broad movement away from deficit-oriented terminology and substantial diversity in how Turkish-speaking autistic adults wish to describe themselves.
The most clearly preferred name for autism was the direct term otizm ("autism"), while otizm spektrumu ("autism spectrum") was the second most frequently endorsed expression.
By contrast, ağır otizm ("profound autism") received little support.

When autism was conceptualised more broadly, nörolojik/beyin farklılığı "neurological/brain difference" was strongly preferred, whereas hastalık "disease" and eksiklik "deficit" were endorsed by very few participants.
Similarly, farklılıklar "differences" was the most frequently endorsed term when discussing both difficulties and strengths.

These findings do not support our expectation that the medicalised and deficit-based discourse historically prominent in Turkish clinical and educational contexts would translate into a predominant preference for medical-model terminology (Doenyas et al., 2023; Dursun et al., 2022).

text.text: Instead, the results suggest that many Turkish-speaking autistic people understand autism through a neurodiversity-informed framework that recognises meaningful challenges without defining autism primarily as pathology.
This pattern is broadly consistent with findings from several other linguistic contexts.

text.text: Thus, although the preferred linguistic form differs across languages, the present findings contribute to a growing crosscultural pattern in which many autistic people favour terminology that is direct, noneuphemistic, and less explicitly deficit-oriented.
At the same time, the findings cannot be reduced to a straightforward preference for identity-first over person-first language.

text.text: The present findings extend this conclusion by demonstrating that the English identity-first/person-first distinction may be particularly difficult to transfer directly into Turkish.
Both otistik kişi and otizmli kişi place the autism-related descriptor before the noun, while the contrast between them is conveyed through morphology and conceptual meaning rather than word order.
Moreover, the more frequently endorsed shortened forms, otistik and otizmli, can refer to a person without an explicit noun.
Consequently, preferences expressed in Turkish should not be interpreted solely through categories developed around English syntax.
The qualitative findings further demonstrate why a binary distinction between identityfirst and person-first language is insufficient.
Autonomy was the most prevalent theme, with participants emphasising that autistic people should determine how they describe themselves.
Participants resisted terminology imposed by clinicians, researchers, organisations, or nonautistic people, even when such terminology was presented as more respectful.

This concern reflects broader critiques of epistemic authority in autism research, whereby non-autistic institutions have historically retained disproportionate influence over how autism and autistic people are represented (Botha, 2021; Botha et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This concern reflects broader critiques of epistemic authority in autism research, whereby non-autistic institutions have historically retained disproportionate influence over how autism and autistic people are represented <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Botha, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Botha et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Participants' accounts therefore suggest that respectful language depends not only on the selected term but also on who selects it and whether autistic people have meaningful control over that choice.
Identity was also central to participants' reasoning.
Many described autism as an inseparable and valued part of who they were, thereby supporting identity-oriented terminology.
Nevertheless, participants often simultaneously emphasised that autism did not constitute the entirety of their identity.
These accounts challenge the assumption that identityfirst language necessarily reduces an individual to a diagnosis.
Instead, participants appeared able to understand autism as an integral aspect of identity while maintaining a broader and multidimensional sense of self.

Similar associations between autistic identity and identity-first language have been observed in Australian samples (Bury, Jellett, Haschek, et al., 2023), while recent research across developmental neurodivergence has likewise found that people may value identity-first terminology because it is concise, accurate, and reflective of lived experience (Pearson et al., 2026).

text.text: Participants also distinguished between the inherent meaning of a term and the social meanings it acquires through use.
Some experienced otistik as uncomfortable because it had been used as an insult or a form of mockery, whereas others deliberately reclaimed the same term to challenge ableism.
Similarly, some participants reported using Asperger or functioning-related terminology strategically because they expected these expressions to attract less stigma or to be more readily understood.
Such preferences should not necessarily be interpreted as endorsement of the conceptual or historical assumptions underlying these labels.
Rather, they may represent pragmatic attempts to manage anticipated prejudice.

This finding illustrates Dwyer's (2022) concept of incommensurability: The same expression may communicate identity, pathology, insult, familiarity, or resistance depending on the speaker, audience, and setting.
The coexistence of quantitative endorsement and qualitative criticism was particularly apparent for Asperger terminology.

Although Asperger-related expressions received moderate quantitative endorsement, several qualitative responses strongly rejected the label because of its historical associations and its perceived role in creating hierarchies among autistic people.
Some participants may continue to use the term because it formed part of their original diagnosis, is familiar to other people, or is perceived as less stigmatising than otistik.
Therefore, aggregate endorsement rates may conceal substantially different motivations for using the same term.

This underscores the value of the mixed-methods design: preference frequencies indicate which terms participants consider usable, whereas qualitative accounts reveal the sometimesconflicting identity-related, historical, and pragmatic considerations underlying their choices.
Participants' criticism of functioning labels provides a related example.

Although "high-functioning" and "low-functioning" received some endorsement, qualitative responses described these labels as overly simplistic, divisive, and potentially harmful because they can obscure fluctuating abilities and support needs.

Several participants preferred support-needs terminology, consistent with previous findings that many autistic people view functioning labels as reductive and favour descriptions that more specifically communicate the type or level of support required (Keates et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Several participants preferred support-needs terminology, consistent with previous findings that many autistic people view functioning labels as reductive and favour descriptions that more specifically communicate the type or level of support required <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Keates et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, support-needs terminology should not itself become a fixed substitute for functioning labels.
Support requirements can differ across domains and contexts, and the present results indicate that even needs-based expressions are not universally preferred.
Wherever possible, specific descriptions of an individual's needs, strengths, and circumstances may therefore be more informative than global categorisations.

In our analyses considering the contribution of individual differences to endorsement, higher negative attitudes towards autism were associated with lower endorsement of terms, on average, for referring to an autistic person, describing autistic identity, and referring to a nonautistic person.

Negative attitudes about autism also predicted lower endorsement of alistik ("allistic"), Nörotipik ("Neurotypical") and Nörotipik kişi ("Neurotypical person"), terms particularly associated with neurodiversity discourse.

By contrast, in-group identification showed a different pattern: those feeling stronger in-group identification tended to endorse alistik ("allistic") and Otizmi olmayan kişi ("Person who does not have autism").

In-group identification was also associated with lower average endorsement of terms to refer to someone's diagnostic status/autistic identity, while internalised stigma was associated with greater average endorsement of terms for referring to an autistic person.

These interpretations remain tentative because the cross-sectional design cannot establish whether attitudes, stigma, and identification shape terminology preferences or are themselves influenced by engagement with particular forms of language and community discourse.
The findings have several implications for researchers, clinicians, educators, media professionals, and advocacy organisations.
First, professionals should ask autistic people which terminology they prefer whenever individual communication is possible.
A person's preferred terminology should not be corrected simply because another expression is considered more professionally conventional or theoretically appropriate.

Second, when writing about groups and individual preferences cannot be obtained, the present findings support the use of direct and non-deficit-oriented Turkish terminology, particularly otizm, while recognising the acceptability of identity-first, person-first, spectrum-based, and neurodiversity-related expressions.

Terms such as "disease," "deficit," "profound autism," and global functioning labels should be used cautiously and only when their meaning is necessary, clearly defined, and acceptable to the people concerned.
Third, terminology should be accompanied by accurate and non-stigmatising representations.
As participants emphasised, replacing one label with another will have limited benefit if underlying ableist attitudes remain unchanged.
Language reform should therefore occur alongside changes in how autistic people are included, supported, and represented.
The study has several strengths.
To our knowledge, it is the first mixed-methods investigation focused specifically on the terminology preferences of Turkish-speaking autistic adults.
The study examined a broad range of expressions rather than limiting the inquiry to identity-first and person-first language.

Recruitment across online and clinical settings and several regions of Türkiye increased the range of perspectives represented, while autistic community consultation contributed to the linguistic and cultural relevance of the materials.

Several limitations should also be acknowledged. Schuck et al. (2025) emphasize that language preferences are shaped by linguistic, cultural, and methodological factors, rather than reflecting a global consensus.

text.text: This study was conducted via convenience sampling and primarily online, which may exclude participants with intellectual disabilities or lower literacy.
Online recruitment may have particularly attracted people already engaged with autism-related or neurodiversity-oriented discussions.

The findings may consequently underrepresent autistic people with intellectual disabilities, nonspeaking autistic people, people with limited internet access, and those who are less connected to autistic communities.

Formal diagnosis and self-identification were also combined, and future adequately powered research should examine whether diagnostic history, age at diagnosis, and mode of identification relate to language preferences.
In addition, only a subset of participants completed the open-ended question.

Although these responses revealed substantial conceptual richness, interviews or focus groups could provide a more detailed examination of how terminology changes across clinical, family, educational, occupational, and online settings.
Future research should prioritise accessible and participatory methods to include autistic people who remain underrepresented in terminology studies.

Comparisons among autistic people, family members, clinicians, educators, and the general public would help identify where differences in terminology may contribute to misunderstanding or unequal power relations.

Research should also investigate how preferences vary according to audience and context, particularly when disclosing a diagnosis, seeking accommodations, communicating with healthcare professionals, or participating in autistic communities.
Coproduced qualitative research could further examine the cultural meanings attached to otistik, otizmli, Asperger, nöroçeşitli, and emerging Turkish terminology.
Such work could inform community-led guidance that remains flexible enough to respect individual choice.
Turkish-speaking autistic people generally preferred direct, difference-based, and nondeficit-oriented language, but there was no universally endorsed way to refer to an autistic person.
Participants' preferences reflected identity and accuracy as well as experiences of stigma, audience expectations, and communicative context.
Most importantly, participants emphasised their right to determine how they are described.
Researchers, clinicians, and other professionals should therefore ask about individual preferences whenever possible and avoid imposing a single terminology on the wider autistic community.
